Most of my clients live in a different time zone than I do.
Jakarta, Berlin, New York, Sydney. For a long time my “system” was a world clock, a to-do app, a spreadsheet for hours and a separate tool for invoices. I kept asking myself the same question every day: what time is it for my client right now, and when should I send this?
So I built the tool I wanted. Meet Taskly  😊 
Under the hood: React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind and Supabase, deployed on Cloudflare. It works offline first, syncs in real time across devices, and every table is protected with Row Level Security.
What I learned: the hardest part of remote freelancing isn’t the work itself. It’s the coordination around it. Good tools should quietly remove that friction.
If you work with clients across time zones, I’d love your feedback. What is the one thing that slows you down the most?

Many investors focus on acquiring land in Indonesia. Fewer focus on whether they could lose it.

Indonesia's new Agrarian Reform Law (Law No. 10 of 2026) may become one of the most important legal developments for businesses with significant landholdings, yet I suspect many investors have not fully considered its implications.

Most commentary has focused on the Law's policy objectives: reducing inequality, resolving agrarian conflicts and supporting agrarian reform. Those objectives are important. However, from an investor's perspective, the more immediate question is:

Could this law affect existing landholdings, future acquisitions, development projects or investment exits?

The answer may be yes.

Why should investors care? The Law introduces:

⚠️ A powerful new agency with authority to resolve agrarian disputes and issue binding decisions.

⚠️Priority agrarian reform areas, potentially affecting land within designated locations.

⚠️ Potential group-wide limits on landholdings, not just limits at the individual company level.

⚠️ New requirements for some HGU holders, particularly those operating large land banks.

For me, the most significant issue is not the text of the Law itself.

It is the fact that many Indonesian transactions already involve some degree of land risk, whether arising from overlapping claims, community occupation, historical use, licensing issues or competing rights. Investors often become focused on valuation, financing and transaction execution, while assuming land matters can be resolved later.

That assumption may become more difficult to make.

If I were advising a private equity fund, infrastructure investor, energy developer, plantation company, industrial estate operator, data center developer or multinational seeking to expand in Indonesia, I would be asking three questions:

1. Which assets could become exposed to agrarian reform measures or conflict claims?

2. Does our current land due diligence adequately identify those risks?

3. How might these issues affect future refinancing, acquisition or exit processes?

The implementing regulations will be critical and are likely to receive close attention from investors over the coming months.

Scientific and Quranic Reflections on Energy in Nature, Ourselves and Clean Energy We Need

From the leaves in our forests to the blood in our veins—and now to the future of zero-carbon hydrogen—one element quietly powers life and industry: Iron (Fe). 🌍🩸⚡

When we look closely at how nature engineers energy, a remarkable unity emerges:

🌱1. Energy in Nature (Plants): Iron is an essential micronutrient that drives chlorophyll synthesis, allowing plants to capture sunlight and convert it into life-sustaining energy.

🩸2. Energy Within Ourselves (Humans): In our bloodstream, iron sits at the core of hemoglobin, binding oxygen in our lungs and delivering it to every cell to fuel ATP production.

🔬3. Shared Molecular Harmony: At the molecular level, the chlorin ring in chlorophyll and the heme group in human blood share a nearly identical porphyrin structure—a striking reminder of the reflection inQuran (51:20–21): "There are countless signs on earth for those with sure faith, as there are within yourselves. Can you not see?"

⚡ 4. Inspiring the Future of Clean Energy:

Beyond sustaining biology, Quran (Al-Hadid 57:25) highlights iron as possessing "Ba'sun Shadid"—mighty power and immense benefits for humankind. Today, modern sustainable engineering is unlocking this exact potential through theSteam-Iron Loop:

Clean Hydrogen Generation: Passing steam (H2O) over metallic iron (Fe) oxidizes it into magnetite (Fe3O4), releasing pure, carbon-free hydrogen (H2).

Circular Energy Storage: Using renewable energy, magnetite can be reduced back into metallic iron—creating a safe, recyclable, high-density energy carrier without the storage hurdles of compressed gas.

At BioCom Indonesia, we believe the best engineering solutions mirror nature’s closed-loop efficiency—turning timeless wisdom and fundamental chemistry into practical, zero-waste infrastructure for a cleaner tomorrow.

- Read receipts and invoices (photo or PDF), extract supplier name, date, amount, item.
- Categorise transactions by type: modal, operasional, gaji, pajak.
- Flag duplicate entries or unusual amounts.
- Prepare a draft profit and loss statement in Rupiah, ready for your review.

- Decide whether a transaction is deductible for PPh or creditable for PPN. That is a tax rule, not a pattern.
- File your SPT. The system needs a qualified person to verify, sign and submit.
- Tell you whether to register for PKP or stay below the threshold. That is strategy, not data entry.
- Replace judgement when two suppliers offer the same product at different terms.

𝗦𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗔𝗣𝗔𝗖 𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀

Recently I've been working with several markets in APAC, from Australia to Southeast Asia. Here are some of my thoughts on what is happening with talent in the region.

1️⃣ 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗴𝘁𝗵𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗔𝗣𝗔𝗖 𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗻𝘁

• APAC leaders often manage very different markets at the same time, for example Australia and Japan together with Vietnam and Indonesia. Each market needs a different approach, so leaders learn to adjust quickly.

• APAC leaders often have to grow the business and deal with uncertainty at the same time. Currency changes, new regulations, fast-changing consumer demand. They learn to keep the business moving even when the situation is not stable.

• Regional teams often include many nationalities and languages. APAC leaders are used to working with people from different cultures and adapting their leadership style.

2️⃣ 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗴𝗹𝗼𝗯𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗶𝗻 𝗔𝗣𝗔𝗖 𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗻𝘁

• Singapore is still the main location for regional leadership teams. India and Malaysia are becoming important hubs for tech, analytics and digital.

• Companies are looking for leaders who can deliver results, lead change and understand digital. Functional expertise alone is not enough anymore.

• I see more APAC leaders moving into global roles. A few years ago, it was usually the other way round: executives came from Europe or the US to lead the region, and then went back to headquarters. Now global companies are starting to see APAC experience as good preparation for bigger roles.

3️⃣ 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗔𝗣𝗔𝗖 𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴

• Hiring from other industries. Consumer companies have started looking for leaders in healthcare, pharma, tech and retail, not only in FMCG.

• Regional digital hubs. Building e-commerce, data and digital marketing teams for the whole region, instead of in every country.

• Preparing APAC leaders for global roles. Giving high-potential leaders experience in both developed and emerging markets, global projects and more exposure to HQ.

• AI skills for business leaders. Not only hiring AI specialists, but also helping commercial and functional leaders use AI in their daily work.

------------------------------------------------------

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗲𝘀?

APAC can be a strong source of future global leaders, if companies give their people the right experience and exposure early.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗮𝘀 𝗮 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲?

So if you’re thinking about a global career, this is a good time to look at APAC, or a growth strategy in the region, as your next career move.
